## TL;DR

Review round 1 correctly identified missing end-to-end coverage for model tests, agent edits, settings import/export, release creation/publication, and release email sending. I returned to the assigned branch, ran the requested actions through the worktree app with browser-side API fixtures, and expanded the QA record. The added interactions surfaced a Settings import feedback bug: applying a settings export refreshed the store in a way that unmounted the panel, hiding its success notice. I fixed the refresh lifecycle, added a regression test, rebuilt the UI, and reran the mocked browser flow. The “Applied” notice now remains visible. No real config was changed, no release was published, and no email was sent.

## Work and rationale

I first read the review report and round 1 evidence, checked the live board state, and confirmed the task had returned to active. The review finding was specific: the original QA note documented navigation but excluded the action paths that proved actual forms and handlers worked. The reviewer recommended isolated fixtures or intercepted requests to exercise those actions without persistent changes or provider calls.

I followed that approach on the auth-less server from this task worktree. I used a 1440 × 1000 Chromium page and intercepted the write/provider endpoints in the browser. The Agent model-test request returned a passing fixture; I added a temporary custom agent and checked that the autosave PATCH contained it. The Settings export control generated a downloadable TOML file; I selected that file, reviewed it, and applied it with `/api/config` intercepted. For Releases, a clean/main fixture enabled the cut flow. I opened the form, entered a version and notes, submitted Publish to an intercepted `/api/release`, and returned a simulated running-to-succeeded result. I also populated a fixture email card for `qa@example.test`, used Send now and confirmed Send, and intercepted `/api/release/email/send` with a simulated sent result. These UI flows reached their request boundaries and displayed their responses without writing config, publishing a release, or sending email.

The import flow exposed a real defect. Its handler correctly sent the PATCH and called `config.load()` to refresh values for any later Settings tab. The normal load path immediately sets `loaded` false. Settings gates the full panel body on that state, so Vue unmounted `SettingsImportExport` before the reload finished. The async handler then updated local refs belonging to the unmounted instance; the user did not see the successful import confirmation. The existing component unit test mounted the child alone and therefore could not reveal this parent lifecycle behavior.

I made `config.load` accept an optional `keepLoaded` flag. Settings import/export uses that option for its post-import refresh, allowing the store’s form data to refresh without hiding the already loaded page. Initial loads and ordinary refreshes retain their previous skeleton behavior. I added a config-store test that holds the refresh request open and asserts that `loaded` stays true while the fresh values are applied. The existing import tests continue to cover download, picked/dropped-file review, PATCH payload, local favorites, and failure behavior.

I reran the browser action flow after rebuilding. It verified the import success notice stays visible, the agent-test fixture renders, the custom-agent PATCH is intercepted, export and import complete, the simulated release success appears, and the simulated email-sent status appears. The run recorded no page errors, console errors, or failed local requests. The updated QA note records both the original four-page navigation/refresh coverage and these additional action flows, along with which external actions were stubbed.

## Approaches tried

- Reviewed the round 1 QA note, automated review report, and round metadata before making changes.
- Tried the separate computer-use Chrome, but it cannot reach the runner’s `127.0.0.1` server. The in-runner Chromium process could connect directly, so I used it for the desktop interaction pass.
- Used browser route interception for `/api/models/test`, `/api/config` PATCH, `/api/release`, `/api/release/run`, `/api/release/notes`, and `/api/release/email/send`. The rest of the app loaded from the actual worktree server.
- Reproduced the import-result loss in the integrated page, then verified the fix in the same browser flow instead of relying only on the child component test.
- Ran `bun run test -- config-store.test.ts settings-import-export.test.ts`; the wrapper reported all selected and always-run cases passing.

## Challenges and blockers

The computer-use Chrome and the task runner are separate browser/network hosts, so that Chrome cannot inspect a server bound to the runner’s loopback address. The in-runner browser fallback used by the initial QA pass and this review follow-up worked. For side-effecting controls, interception was necessary to exercise the actual Vue controls while keeping writes, publication, email, and model provider calls isolated. The temporary browser harness and all intercepted data stayed under ignored `.repoos/` state; the committed QA record contains summarized results rather than configuration contents.

The test wrapper ran four test files because the repository adds always-run safety tests to the two requested selections. The result was green. `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` then passed, including remote scoped validation and the local UI smoke test. Build output is ignored and was not staged.

## Key learnings

Testing a child component in isolation can miss lifecycle behavior controlled by its parent. Here, a store refresh toggled a page-level loading flag, and the parent unmounted the component before it could display a result. When an async UI action must refresh shared state, verify whether that refresh changes the parent’s mount conditions. A keep-visible refresh option gives callers a way to update loaded forms without replacing them with a skeleton.

Mocking the final API boundary is useful for QA controls whose real behavior could write project state, publish a release, email recipients, or call a provider. A convincing check should click the actual control, assert the request’s important fields, return a representative response, and confirm the UI outcome. That gives stronger evidence than a static view inventory while avoiding the side effect under test.
